reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A major cause of spontaneous lobar intracerebral haemorrhage in older adults, typically sparing the deep grey structures affected by hypertensive haemorrhage
Susceptibility-weighted MRI reveals lobar cerebral microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis, which are key imaging biomarkers
Transient focal neurological episodes, sometimes called amyloid spells, can mimic transient ischaemic attacks or seizures and are associated with superficial siderosis
Progressive cognitive impairment is common, and the condition frequently coexists with Alzheimer disease pathology
The Boston criteria integrate clinical and imaging features to estimate the probability of cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy substantially raise the risk of further haemorrhage and require careful individual risk assessment
A rare inflammatory form, cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation, presents with subacute encephalopathy and oedematous white matter change that may respond to immunosuppression
reference.pathophysiology: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is caused by progressive deposition of amyloid-beta protein within the walls of small and medium-sized arteries and arterioles of the cerebral cortex and leptomeninges. The amyloid-laden vessels become fragile and prone to rupture, producing lobar haemorrhages, microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis from repeated small bleeds, and impaired vascular function contributes to cognitive decline. The same amyloid-beta peptide is central to Alzheimer disease, explaining the frequent overlap, and an immune reaction against vascular amyloid can produce the inflammatory subtype. Deposition of vascular amyloid also underlies the amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) seen with anti-amyloid antibody therapies.
additionalDifferentials: Haemorrhage from an underlying tumour or vascular malformation
Hypertensive or other microangiopathy causing microbleeds
Ischaemic stroke or transient ischaemic attack when presenting with transient episodes
Primary or secondary CNS vasculitis in the inflammatory subtype
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome with cortical bleeding
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain including susceptibility-weighted imaging to detect lobar microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis
CT of the head in the acute setting to identify and localise haemorrhage
Blood pressure assessment and coagulation studies to evaluate contributing factors
Vascular imaging to exclude an underlying structural lesion in appropriate cases
Amyloid PET and cerebrospinal fluid amyloid and tau markers where cognitive assessment or Alzheimer overlap is relevant
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis and, rarely, biopsy when the inflammatory subtype is suspected
redFlags: Acute lobar intracerebral haemorrhage with rising intracranial pressure or deteriorating consciousness
Recurrent haemorrhage, particularly in patients on antithrombotic therapy
Subacute encephalopathy with oedematous white matter change suggesting the inflammatory subtype
Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities developing during anti-amyloid antibody treatment
reference.prognosis: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy carries a high risk of recurrent lobar haemorrhage and progressive cognitive decline, with prognosis depending on haemorrhage burden and comorbidity; the inflammatory subtype may improve with immunosuppression, but there is no disease-modifying treatment for the underlying angiopathy.
pitfalls: Prescribing anticoagulants or antiplatelets without weighing the elevated haemorrhage risk in known or suspected cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Misinterpreting transient focal episodes as transient ischaemic attacks and starting antithrombotic therapy
Overlooking the treatable inflammatory subtype in a patient with subacute encephalopathy and white matter oedema
Failing to recognise amyloid-related imaging abnormalities as a caveat of anti-amyloid antibody therapy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Avoid antithrombotics where possible, carefully weighing and generally withholding anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents given the high lobar haemorrhage risk
Optimise blood pressure control to reduce recurrent lobar intracerebral haemorrhage
Manage acute lobar haemorrhage with supportive neurocritical care, reversal of any anticoagulation and neurosurgical evaluation
Treat the inflammatory subtype (amyloid-related angiitis) with corticosteroids and further immunosuppression
Control seizures and amyloid spells with antiseizure medication, avoiding misdiagnosis as transient ischaemic attack and inappropriate anticoagulation
Exercise caution with anti-amyloid antibody therapies owing to the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, and provide cognitive assessment and dementia support
Refer to neurology or stroke services and undertake surveillance susceptibility-weighted MRI for microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis
